notes:
I've put together notes on Job 38:1–20, but some parts of your request aren't covered:

- **Missing views:** I found nothing on these verses from Catholic or Orthodox sites (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org), from Lutheran sites (lcms.org, 1517.org), or about prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching. Those are left out.
- **Modern scholarship is thin:** apart from one NET Bible note (v. 13), the modern scholars below are only quoted secondhand inside older commentaries.
- **Verse 1 has the most material.** I ran out of searches before checking Gill, Ellicott and Matthew Henry verse by verse, so verses 5–11 and 16–20 lean mostly on the Pulpit Commentary and Enduring Word.
- **Two pages were read in full without line markers:** the Pulpit Commentary (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-38.html) and Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-38/). Notes taken from them have the URL but no citation tag.

---

**v. 1 — The LORD answers out of the whirlwind**
- *Traditional:* Ellicott calls this chapter the climax of the poem. The questions could only be settled by the One whose rule was being disputed, and he speaks from the storm Elihu had described. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/38-1.htm
- Guzik (Enduring Word, the Calvary Chapel teacher on your list): God has said nothing directly since chapter 2. He now speaks only to Job, perhaps because Job was the only one who actually prayed to God.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-38/
- Guzik, quoting Andersen: Job's troubles began when a great wind killed his children, and God now speaks from a storm.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-38/
- Matthew Henry: God's voice could be heard clearly even through the noise of the storm. He sometimes answers his people with severe correction, but always rightly.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_038.cfm
- Clarke (Methodist): the Hebrew word means a violent storm, meant to fill Job with awe. He also notes that the old Aramaic paraphrase (the Targum) reads "a whirlwind of grief," which makes the scene inward and symbolic.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/38-1.html
- *Who is speaking?* Gill (Baptist) says it is God the Son, the eternal Word, probably appearing in human form.  Wesley's Notes also call him "the eternal word."  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/38-1.html ; https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nas/job/38-1.html
- *Is this Elihu's storm?* Most say yes. The Cambridge Bible disagrees: "the" before "storm" is general, meaning simply that God spoke out of a storm.  Coffman also says no, because Elihu's last words describe the storm dying down.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/38-1.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/38-1.html
- *Authorship question:* The Pulpit Commentary argues that "the whirlwind" points back to Elihu's speech (37:9), which supports chapters 32–37 being original to the book.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-38.html

**v. 2 — "Who is this who obscures My counsel…?"**
- *Disagreement over who is meant:*
  - G. Campbell Morgan, quoted by Guzik, thinks it was Elihu. Guzik adds that every speaker in the book spoke without knowing what chapters 1–2 reveal.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-38/
  - John Piper (Desiring God, Baptist) says it was Job, because in 42:3 Job quotes this line and applies it to himself.  https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/job-the-revelation-of-god-in-suffering
  - Matthew Henry admits it could seem aimed at Elihu, but Job rightly took it to himself.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_038.cfm
- Pulpit Commentary: God ignores Elihu and rebukes Job. Job had cast doubt on God's moral government, his mercy and nearly his justice. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-38.html
- Dunagan: the first thing Job hears from God is a rebuke.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dun/job-38.html

**v. 3 — "Brace yourself like a man"**
- Pulpit: God grants the court hearing Job had demanded (9:32–35; 13:3; 31:35). When it comes, Job backs down (40:4–5). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-38.html
- Guzik: this is not only a rebuke. God has finally shown up, and that is a great comfort to Job. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-38/
- Coffman: the questions are a loving correction, not meant to humiliate. God did not scold Job for searching.  https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/cjb/job/38-4.html
- *A different emphasis:* Barnes says God's aim is to bring Job to a right frame of mind before he defends him, so at first he seems only to rebuke.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/38-1.htm

**v. 4 — "Where were you…?"**
- Barnes: Job did not yet exist, so he could not have helped or advised God. "Laid the foundations" is building language, not a description of how the earth was actually made.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/38-4.htm
- Matthew Poole and Benson: God made the world without Job's help, so he can run it without Job's advice.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/38-4.htm
- Geneva Bible notes (Reformed): if Job cannot judge what happened before he was born, he cannot grasp the hidden causes of God's judgments.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/38-4.htm
- Gill: the earth's only "foundations" are God's power and will.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/38-4.html
- Pulpit: picturing creation as a building is a concession to human weakness, because creation itself is beyond imagining.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/38-4.htm

**vv. 5–6 — Measurements, line, footings, cornerstone**
- Dunagan: the earth is pictured as a building with foundation, dimensions, measuring line, footings and cornerstone.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dun/job-38.html
- Benson: if Job does not understand these visible works, he should not claim to understand God's hidden providence.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/38-4.htm
- Pulpit: "Surely you know!" is irony. The building details are not to be pressed too far, and the cornerstone is the finishing touch. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-38.html
- Matthew Henry applies the cornerstone to Christ, who is both foundation and cornerstone of redemption.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/38-4.htm

**v. 7 — Morning stars and sons of God**
- *Traditional:* Keil & Delitzsch: no human was there, but the angels watched with joy, as people did when the temple foundation was laid (Ezra 3:10).  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/38-4.htm
- Clarke (Methodist): both phrases mean the angels, created before the visible world.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/38-7.html
- Gill: they are God's sons by creation, not by birth like Christ or by adoption like believers.  https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/job/38-7.html
- *Different reading:* The Pulpit Commentary takes the "morning stars" as the actual stars, singing a silent song of praise. Only the "sons of God" are angels. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-38.html
- Guzik goes further: since "all" the sons of God rejoiced, Lucifer must have fallen some time after the earth was made. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-38/
- Poole, quoted by Guzik: the angels praised God's work and did not criticise it, as Job had criticised his providence. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-38/

**vv. 8–11 — The sea held behind doors**
- Guzik: probably the second day of creation (Genesis 1:6–8). Quoting Smick, he notes that in the ancient Semitic world, mastering the raging sea was a mark of divine power. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-38/
- Piper paraphrases God's point: it was I, not you, who set the sea's limits.  https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/job-the-revelation-of-god-in-suffering
- Pulpit: the newborn sea is wrapped in cloud and darkness to show it was under its Maker's control from the start. It calls this an independent, poetic account of creation, not taken wholly from Genesis. "Doors and bars" are like barred city gates. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-38.html
- Bridgeway Bible Commentary: God separated the waters above from the waters below and made dry land appear.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/38-13.html

**vv. 12–13 — Commanding the dawn; the wicked shaken out**
- *Traditional:* Barnes: the wicked do their deeds at night, and the morning light scatters them.  https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/cev/job/38-13.html
- Ellicott: the picture is of someone shaking out a cloth.  Pulpit: being "shaken from the earth" is Eastern exaggeration.  https://biblehub.com/job/38-13.htm
- Cambridge Bible: the dawn grabs the edges of night's blanket and shakes the wicked out. The dawn is not just a natural event but a moral one.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/38-13.htm
- Poole: morning was also the usual time for carrying out judgment (Psalm 101:8).  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/38-13.htm
- Guzik's point: has Job ever made the morning come even once? https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-38/
- *Christian applications:*
  - Gill applies the dawn to the gospel spreading to the ends of the earth.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/38-13.htm
  - Matthew Henry links it to the "dayspring" of Luke 1:78.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/38-13.html
  - Grant (a dispensationalist commentator) applies it to the dawning millennium, when Christ will expose the wicked.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/job-38.html
- *Modern note:* The NET Bible note: night is like a blanket over the earth, shaken out at dawn, and the wicked who work at night are shaken out with it.  https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=job&chapter=38&verse=13
- Coffman says Marvin Pope's translation hints at the Flood.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/38-13.html

**v. 14 — Clay under a seal; folds of a garment**
- Keil & Delitzsch: the dawn is like a signet ring stamping clay. Shapes hidden in the dark become visible, each in its own colour.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/38-13.htm
- Pulpit: ancient seals were pressed into clay. Morning turns a shapeless mass into a varied surface, like the pattern raised on an embroidered robe. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-38.html
- Clarke thinks v. 15 belongs straight after v. 13, and v. 14 interrupts the thought.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/38-13.html

**v. 15 — Light withheld; the raised arm broken**
- *Traditional:* For the wicked, darkness is their "light." When dawn takes it away, their raised arm is broken: they are caught and punished.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-38.html
- Keil & Delitzsch: sunrise takes away their darkness and their planned evil is foiled.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/38-13.htm
- *Another view:* Constable reports a reading that the verse is ironic: God controls the wicked rather than destroying them. He cites the Jewish scholar Tsevat, who says the daily chance to punish the wicked is not in fact used.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/38-13.html
- *Jewish tradition:* The Hebrew word for "wicked" here is written with a raised letter. Keil & Delitzsch report the Midrash explaining it: the rich wicked will become poor, or God takes away their sight.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/38-13.htm

**v. 16 — Springs of the sea; the deep**
- Pulpit: "springs" means the deepest sources. Job cannot get to the bottom of anything, and deep-sea dredging brings us no closer to the sea's origin. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-38.html
- Guzik: Job probably did not even know there were springs in the sea. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-38/

**v. 17 — Gates of death**
- Pulpit: the gates of death mean Sheol, the place of the dead (10:21–22; 17:16). The second line just repeats the first. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-38.html
- Pulpit homiletics: for saint and sinner alike, life after death is an unfathomable mystery.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-38.html
- Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel) links it to Job's wish to rest in death: Job, have you been there?  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/csc/job-38.html

**v. 18 — The extent of the earth**
- Pulpit: Job probably thought of the earth as a vast plain of unknown size. "Tell Me, if you know" looks back to vv. 4–5. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-38.html
- Barnes, writing on v. 13, says the Bible's language about the earth's edges assumes the earth is a plain with limits.  https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/cev/job/38-13.html

**vv. 19–20 — The home of light and darkness**
- Guzik, quoting Andersen: light and darkness are pictured as mysterious beings that need a guide home. God can be that guide; Job cannot. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-38/
- Pulpit: light is separate from the sun (Genesis 1:3, 16). Job himself spoke of a "land of darkness" (10:21–22), so can he point to where it is? Only God can keep light and darkness within their bounds (Genesis 1:4). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-38.html
- Bridgeway: can Job take the sun to rise each morning and lead it to rest at night?  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/38-13.html

**Whole passage — does God answer Job's question?**
- Constable: God says nothing about Job's suffering or the problem of evil and offers no defence. He simply reveals himself.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/38-1.html
- Coffman: since God lists no sins, Job's suffering was not punishment. Yet God never tells Job about the scene with Satan.  https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nas/job/38-1.html
- Pulpit (E. Johnson) offers an answer: God may send suffering to test and purify the righteous.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-38.html
